Constance Garnett was an English translator whose prodigious output of Russian literature in the early twentieth century introduced English readers to Dostoevsky, Tolstoy, Chekhov, and Turgenev. Over a forty-year career she translated more than seventy volumes, establishing the canonical English versions of Russian classics and shaping how the Anglophone world read Russian fiction for generations.

Garnett was trained as a classicist at Cambridge, one of the few women to earn honors in Classics. Her precision with grammar and syntax later defined her translation practice. She began translating Russian in eighteen ninety-two, initially from necessity. Her husband was imprisoned for radical politics, and she worked to support the family. She translated the complete works of Dostoevsky, including Crime and Punishment and The Brothers Karamazov, and Tolstoy, including War and Peace and Anna Karenina. She also translated Chekhov and many others across multiple decades.

Her translations were elegant, readable English that prioritized fluency and emotional resonance over literal fidelity. Modern scholars note she sometimes smoothed or compressed Russian style. Though she worked from Russian without prior philological training, relying on native Russian speakers and her own linguistic intuition, her later work is considered more accurate than her early efforts. She published a total of seventy-one volumes of Russian literature, often working simultaneously on multiple texts at a pace that was almost superhuman. Her versions became so canonical that English readers of the twentieth century encountered Russian literature through Garnett's lens, a dominance later translators struggled to overcome.
